lesson.title: One Peak, One Story: What Unimodal Distributions Reveal
lesson.summary: A unimodal distribution has a single clear peak where data cluster most densely, making it the most common shape for describing a single underlying process or population.
lesson.body:
A unimodal distribution has exactly one clear peak, one region of the number line where data values pile up more densely than anywhere else, with the bars or points thinning out steadily as you move away from that peak in either direction. The word "unimodal" literally means "one mode" in the sense of one major cluster, and it describes the number of humps in a graph, which is a completely separate question from whether the distribution is symmetric or skewed.

This distinction matters because shape has more than one dimension. Every distribution discussed so far in this unit, the symmetric quiz-score example, the left-skewed exam scores, and the right-skewed home prices, was also unimodal: each had a single peak, just with a different balance of the tails around it. A distribution can be unimodal and symmetric, unimodal and skewed left, or unimodal and skewed right. Modality answers "how many peaks," while skew answers "which direction does the imbalance point," and you need both descriptions to fully characterize a graph's shape.

Consider twenty-two students' scores on a test, grouped into ten-point intervals: 2 students scored in the 60s, 5 in the 70s, 10 in the 80s, 4 in the 90s, and 1 scored 100. If you sketch this as a histogram, the bars rise from 2, to 5, to a peak of 10 in the 80s interval, then fall to 4 and then 1. There is exactly one interval where the bars reach their maximum height, the 80s, with 10 out of 22 students, close to half the class, falling in that single interval, and the counts decrease steadily as you move away from it in either direction. That single rise then fall pattern is what makes this distribution unimodal.

It helps to distinguish this general sense of "one peak" from the more specific mode, a single most-frequent exact value covered later in this unit. Unimodal describes the overall silhouette of a histogram, a broad region where data concentrates, while the mode is a narrower idea that usually applies to distinct, repeatable values, such as an exact test score earned by more students than any other exact score. A distribution can be unimodal, with one clear region of concentration, even if no single exact value repeats often enough to stand out as an obvious mode.

Unimodal distributions are the most common shape you will encounter because they typically arise when a single underlying process generates the data. Human heights within one sex and age group, reaction times on a simple task, and scores on a well-designed test all tend to cluster around one typical value with fewer and fewer cases as you move further from it, producing one dominant peak rather than several.

When a graph instead shows two separated peaks, it is usually a signal that two different groups or processes have been combined into a single data set, which is precisely the situation explored next under bimodal distributions. Recognizing unimodal shape first gives you a baseline: once you know what a single, cleanly clustered peak looks like, an unexpected second peak becomes a visible and meaningful clue rather than something you might overlook.
